name: Fairchild Micrologic electrical-isolation approach
summary: Fairchild engineers separated the parts of a chip electrically with diffused p–n junctions, a manufacturable way to build working integrated circuits.
description: The Fairchild Micrologic approach of electrically isolating semiconductor circuit regions; Haas and Kattner’s working boron-diffused p–n junction-isolated flip-flops of September 1960 are early physical witnesses.
tier_reason: The isolation approach is more than a single sold specimen; preserve its uncertain exact chronology separately. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.

date.label: 27 Sep 1960
date.basis: Working boron-diffused isolation circuits dated 27 September; public Micrologic announcement followed March 1961.

events.statement: Haas and Kattner’s boron-diffusion isolation process produced working flip-flop circuits using p–n junction separation.
events.caveats: This is not the claim that all integrated circuits require p–n junction isolation.

date.label: by 1960-11-01
date.basis: Latest documented community-use or recognition bound; no earliest date is established.

events.statement: Fairchild R&D engineer James Nall favorably assessed electrical isolation for Micrologic by 1 November 1960, following the reported diffused-isolation flip-flops.
events.scope: Fairchild Micrologic electrical isolation of semiconductor circuit regions, with working boron-diffused junction-isolated flip-flops reported in the same development chronology.
events.caveats: Nall evaluates electrical isolation in general; the quoted report excerpt does not identify the exact flip-flop specimen. Its association with the diffused approach is drawn from the participant chronology. The 1961 Type F die has not been identified as this specimen.

evidence.locator: Printed p. 33, September and November 1960 chronology quoting R&D reports
evidence.supports: Identifies successful September diffused-isolation flip-flops and Nall’s 1 November 1960 favorable assessment of the electrical isolation method.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. Latest documented community-use or recognition bound; no earliest date is established. community_entry.community: Fairchild R&D engineer James Nall and Micrologic development team
community_entry.rationale: A named engineer’s favorable assessment of electrical isolation within the Micrologic team supplies actual specialist recognition of the refined method beyond the September initial tests.
community_entry.caveats: Nall evaluates electrical isolation in general; the quoted report excerpt does not identify the exact flip-flop specimen. Its association with the diffused approach is drawn from the participant chronology. The 1961 Type F die has not been identified as this specimen.

caveats: Nall’s assessment addresses electrical isolation as a method and does not identify a particular flip-flop specimen; a later commercial Type F circuit is not assumed to be identical.

links.statement: The same flip-flop programme progressed from physical isolation to a working junction-isolated production approach.
links.alternatives: Epoxy-filled channels and p–n junctions are alternative ways to separate components.
links.caveats: No claim that the May device caused the underlying junction-isolation idea.
links.timing: Exact dates establish May before September despite equal year anchors.

evidence.supports: Sequential working implementations and preferred isolation method.
